definition: Rules that create legal obligations and can be enforced, such as treaties, statutes and regulations.
why: Determines whether non-compliance can lead to fines, litigation or state responsibility.

definition: Non-binding instruments such as declarations, principles, guidelines and codes of conduct that shape behaviour without legal force.
why: Often the first step toward binding rules, and the main tool where consensus for a treaty is missing.

definition: An AI system used in areas where errors can seriously affect people, such as hiring, credit, health, policing or critical infrastructure.
why: Triggers the heaviest obligations under risk-based laws like the EU AI Act and the Colorado AI Act.

definition: A model trained on broad data that can perform many different tasks and be built into many downstream applications.
why: The EU AI Act gives these models their own set of obligations, separate from use-case rules.

definition: Risk from a very capable general-purpose model that could have significant effects at scale, for example on public safety or security.
why: Models judged to pose it face extra evaluation, incident reporting and cybersecurity duties.

definition: The most advanced general-purpose AI models at a given time, whose capabilities may outpace understanding of their risks.
why: The focus of the summit series, the G7 Hiroshima Process and laws such as California SB 53.

definition: A weapon system that, once activated, can select and engage targets without further human intervention.
why: Subject of the CCW talks and UN General Assembly resolutions. There is no agreed definition.

definition: The idea that humans must keep enough understanding of and influence over a weapon system's use of force to remain legally and morally accountable.
why: A central concept in autonomous weapons debates. States use different wording, such as appropriate human judgement.

definition: A proposed structure for regulating autonomous weapons: prohibit systems that cannot be used in line with international law, and place limits on all others.
why: Frames much of the CCW rolling text and many national positions.

definition: The law of armed conflict, including the principles of distinction, proportionality and precaution.
why: The baseline standard against which military uses of AI are assessed.

definition: The policies, roles, processes and controls an organisation uses to govern AI, as specified by ISO/IEC 42001.
why: Makes AI governance systematic and auditable, and can be certified.

definition: Governance, risk and compliance applied to AI: the function that turns laws, standards and policies into controls and evidence inside an organisation.
why: Connects the rules in this register to what an organisation actually does.

definition: AI systems that can plan and take actions, such as calling tools, accessing data or triggering transactions, with some degree of autonomy.
why: Acting rather than only generating text raises new questions of authority, permissions and human accountability.

definition: Roles under the EU AI Act: the provider develops an AI system or places it on the market; the deployer uses it under its own authority.
why: Most obligations depend on which role an organisation plays for a given system.

definition: An attack in which crafted input makes a language model ignore its instructions or take unintended actions.
why: The top risk in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, and especially serious when models can use tools.
